meta.description: Not Satchel Paige. The line is a Gunning King cartoon caption in Punch, 24 October 1906 — and the joke was already in US newspapers in February 1905.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sometimes I sits and thinks, and sometimes I just sits'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to a Punch cartoon of 24 Oct 1906 and to an anonymous Maine fisherman in Feb 1905 — years before Satchel Paige was ever credited.

answer.label: Not Satchel Paige — a Punch cartoon caption from 1906
answer.sourceLine: The famous wording is the caption of a cartoon by Gunning King in the British humour magazine Punch, 24 October 1906: an old man tells the vicar’s wife, “sometimes I sits and thinks and then again I just sits.” The joke was already in American newspapers by February 1905, credited to an anonymous Maine fisherman — so nobody can claim it outright, and Satchel Paige was a four-month-old baby when the Punch cartoon ran.
answer.confidenceText: Documented in print decades before Paige was quoted on it; no evidence he originated the line.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: February 1905 US newspapers, crediting an anonymous Maine fisherman

source.excerpt:
Vicar’s wife: Now that you can’t get about and are not able to read, how do you manage to occupy the time?
Rustic man: Well, mum, sometimes I sits and thinks and then again I just sits.
trail: February 1905 — the earliest match Quote Investigator located: The Pittsburg Press and The Buffalo Sunday News, crediting The Boston Record, report a Maine fisherman’s reply, “Oh, sometimes I sit and think, and then again I just sit.” QI, 29 Aug 2018 ↗
24 October 1906 — the Punch cartoon by Gunning-King fixes the dialect form “sometimes I sits and thinks,” and reprints carry it worldwide. Wikiquote, Punch, Vol. 131, p. 297 ↗
1915 — L. M. Montgomery puts a variant in Mrs. Skinner’s mouth in Chapter XXX of Anne of the Island: “Part of the time I sits and thinks and the rest I jest sits.” Project Gutenberg full text ↗
2006 and 2009 — the line is reassigned, first to Winnie-the-Pooh in the Chicago Tribune, then to Satchel Paige in a Wisconsin newspaper, with no evidence offered either time. QI ↗
source.excerptNote: The caption of a Gunning King cartoon showing the vicar’s wife visiting a rustic old man laid up with an injured foot. The familiar modern wording — “and sometimes I just sits” — is a smoothed-down descendant of this.

sourceLink.text: Wikiquote: the Punch cartoon, with volume and page

source.rightsNote: Every documented appearance of this saying is comfortably pre-1931 and in the public domain in the United States: the February 1905 newspaper items, the Punch cartoon caption of 24 October 1906, and L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of the Island (1915). The exact modern wording — “and sometimes I just sits” — is an anonymous folk variant with no identified owner, so there is no rights holder to name.

author.name: William Gunning King
author.heading: About William Gunning King
author.bio: William Gunning King was a British painter and illustrator, trained at South Kensington and the Royal Academy Schools, who exhibited widely in London and drew regularly for Punch, The Graphic and the Windsor Magazine. He specialised in rural and animal subjects, and his gently observed country characters are exactly the register of the 1906 cartoon whose caption became this saying. He is best described as the man who gave the line its famous form, not its inventor — the same joke was circulating anonymously in newspapers a year earlier.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: A line this quotable and this ownerless gets reassigned to whoever fits the mood. The two standing claimants are a baseball legend and a stuffed bear.

items.why: Quote Investigator found the Paige credit in a 2009 Wisconsin newspaper with no historical basis presented ↗. Paige was born on 7 July 1906 — barely three months before the Punch cartoon, and a year after the saying first appeared in US newspapers. Wikiquote’s Satchel Paige page ↗ does not carry the line at all.
A 2006 Chicago Tribune piece handed the line to Pooh, but as QI notes ↗, Milne’s first Pooh book did not appear until 1926 — twenty years after the saying was already in print.

Montgomery gave the mail-cart driver Mrs. Skinner the line “Part of the time I sits and thinks and the rest I jest sits” in Chapter XXX of Anne of the Island, 1915 ↗. That is her borrowing a circulating joke, not coining it.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: an anonymous saying, first documented in February 1905 newspapers and given its famous wording by a Gunning King cartoon in Punch, 24 October 1906 ↗.

context.heading: A rustic joke that outlived everyone who told it
lead: The line works because it refuses to apologise. Asked what he does with his time, an old man laid up with a bad foot answers that half of it goes on thinking and the other half on nothing at all — and he says it without a trace of shame. That is a very early-1900s English comic type, and it is exactly the sort of country character Gunning King drew for Punch for a decade.

Once a line is that good and that anonymous, it drifts. It shows up in L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of the Island in 1915 in the mouth of a chatty mail-cart driver, then attaches itself over the century to whoever the reader most enjoys imagining saying it — Winnie-the-Pooh, or a legendarily laconic pitcher.
context.pull: Satchel Paige was four months old when the Punch cartoon ran.
